Radial Head and Neck Fractures
 CORE
July 31, 2026
Alexander Aleem, MD (2020–present)
Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Understand the common etiology of radial head/neck fractures.
Perform appropriate clinical and radiographic assessment of radial head/neck fractures.
Determine appropriate indications for the nonsurgical and surgical management of radial
head/neck fractures.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Radial head/neck fractures can occur in isolation; however, they often are associated with
more complex injuries, such as elbow fractures-dislocations, and/or soft-tissue injuries.1-4
The radial head plays an important role as a secondary valgus stabilizer of the elbow.1,3,5




NOTES

1/25

Epidemiology
The most common elbow fracture3
Approximately 20% of all elbow fractures involve the radial head/neck.
3:2 ratio of women to men2,3
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The radial head has a variable elliptical shape with a concave proximal surface that articulates
with the capitellum5 (Figure 1).
The slightly flatter margin articulates with the lesser sigmoid notch to form the proximal
radioulnar joint along the radial neck.
Figure 1 AP (A) and lateral (B) view photographs of a bone model show the three bones that form
the elbow joint. The blue arrows point to the radial head. (Reproduced with permission from
Domes C: Radial head fracture. Rosemont, IL, Orthopaedic Trauma Association. Available at:
https://ota.org/for-patients/find-info-body-part/3733. Accessed January 26, 2023.)

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The noncircular anatomy and variable offset of the head relative to the neck results in a
small amount of translation that occurs at the radiocapitellar and proximal radioulnar
joints. The radial head contributes notably to elbow stability, especially in combination
with other injuries.1 Excision of the radial head leads to an abnormal transfer of axial
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:56 PM
AAOS | Radial Head and Neck Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000660
2/25

forces across the ulnohumeral joint and alters the proximal radioulnar joint.6,7 The main
extraosseous blood supply is provided by an arterial ring, which is formed around the
radial neck by the radial recurrent artery and branches from the ulnar artery. A so-called
safe zone, in which potential hardware can be placed without risk of impingement on the
ulna, consists of the 90° arc of non-articular cartilage of the radial head centered on a
point 10° anterior to the lateral aspect of the radial head with the forearm in neutral
rotation and can allow for plating down the radial neck/shaft1,8,9 (Figure 2).
Figure 2 Illustration of the elbow shows the safe zone for hardware placement in radial
head fractures. (Reproduced with permission from Morgan WJ: Fractures of the radial
head. J Hand Surg Am 2001;1[4]:225-35.)
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Radial head/neck fractures typically result from a fall onto an outstretched hand with the
forearm in pronation, which results in an axial load on the elbow.
Higher energy trauma may result in a higher degree of associated injuries.2,3,10,11
Risk Factors
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:56 PM
AAOS | Radial Head and Neck Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000660
3/25

Lower energy injuries typically occur in women with risk factors for osteoporosis.2,3
Injury Classification
The Mason classification of radial head fractures is shown in Table 1 and Figure 3.
Type II fractures are displaced more than 2 mm and involve more than 30% of the articular
surface.
High interobserver variability in classification system, even with use of advanced imaging
studies12
Table 1 Modified Mason Classification of Radial Head Fracture
Fracture Type
Characteristics
Type I
Nondisplaced or minimally displaced <2 mm; no mechanical block to
motion
Type II
Displaced >2 mm or angulated; possible mechanical block to forearm
rotation
Type III
Comminuted and displaced; mechanical block to motion
Type IV
Radial head fracture with associated elbow dislocation
Adapted from Dehghan N, McKee MD: Fractures of the elbow, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS
Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2020, pp 931-943.

Figure 3 Illustrations show the Mason classification of radial head fractures. A, Type I,
nondisplaced fracture. B, Type II, displaced partial articular fracture. C, Type III, comminuted
fracture. D, Type IV injury, indicating an associated ipsilateral ulnohumeral dislocation.
(Reproduced from Mathew PK, Athwal GS, King GJW: Terrible triad injury of the elbow: Current
concepts. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2009;17[3]:137-151.)
Associated Injuries
Associated injuries are related to patient age and mechanism of injury.
They are more common in patients with higher energy injuries.2,3,10,11
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:56 PM
AAOS | Radial Head and Neck Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000660
5/25


Associated Injuries
Associated injuries are related to patient age, mechanism of injury, and fracture
complexity. Kaas et al10,11 reported associated injuries in as many as 76% of patients
with a radial head fracture evaluated via MRI. Type III fractures or fractures with
complete loss of contact between the radial head and the capitellum are often
associated with a concomitant elbow dislocation.4,13 Other associated injuries include
collateral ligament injuries, coronoid fractures, and capitellar injuries. Despite the high
rate of concomitant injuries observed on MRI, most do not influence management.11
The main exceptions are associated elbow dislocations or terrible triad injuries
(associated elbow dislocation and coronoid fractures), which are historically associated
with poor outcomes.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Fractures of the radial head/neck typically occur after a fall onto an outstretched hand.
The patient should be questioned about ipsilateral wrist, forearm, or shoulder pain.
Physical Examination
Pain with palpation over the radial head
The surgeon should examine elbow range of motion (ROM) and assess for a block to
pronation/supination or flexion/extension.

Physical Examination
The surgeon should examine the forearm, wrist, and elbow for tenderness along the
course of the interosseous membrane (Essex-Lopresti lesion), instability of the distal
radioulnar joint, pain at the medial side of the elbow (medial collateral ligament), and
pain at the lateral side of the elbow (lateral collateral ligament). Lateral elbow pain and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:56 PM
AAOS | Radial Head and Neck Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000660
6/25

tenderness or limitations in elbow or forearm motion should alert the examiner to a
possible radial head fracture.
Neurovascular Examination
A thorough neurovascular examination should be performed. Specific attention should be paid
to posterior interosseous and ulnar nerve function.
Neurovascular injuries are rare in patients with a lower energy injury.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
AP and lateral radiographs of the elbow are routinely obtained.

Radiography
Standard elbow radiographs usually are adequate for the assessment of radial
head/neck fractures. Nondisplaced fractures of the radial head/neck may not be visible;
however, they may be diagnosed by elevation of the anterior and posterior fat pads (the
sail sign; Figure 4) from intra-articular hemarthrosis.14,15 This is more likely to be
observed in pediatric patients. Additional imaging studies include a radiocapitellar view
(Figure 5), which is obtained by positioning for a lateral view but angling the x-ray tube
45° toward the shoulder, Shoulder, forearm, and wrist radiographs may be required
depending on patient history and physical examination findings; however, the joint
above and below an injury should be routinely imaged.

(arrows). (Reproduced from Armstrong AD: Fracture of the distal humerus, in Sarwark JF,
ed: Essentials of Musculoskeletal Care, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2010, pp 361-363.)

Figure 5 Radiocapitellar radiograph of the elbow. (Courtesy of Alexander Aleem, MD, St.
Louis, MO.)
Computed Tomography
For comminuted fractures, a CT scan may delineate the location, number, and size of the
fragments and is rapidly emerging as a standard imaging modality for more complicated radial
head fractures12 (Figure 6). Surface-rendered three-dimensional CT reconstruction aids in
planning for surgical reconstruction.
Figure 6 Three-dimensional CT reconstruction image of an elbow shows a comminuted radial
head fracture and a small coronoid tip fracture. (Reproduced with permission from Yoon A,
Athwal GS, Faber KJ, King GJ: Radial head fractures. J Hand Surg Am 2012;37[12]:2626-2634.)
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is useful for detecting associated ligamentous injuries.
Not routinely used because the additional information obtained via MRI usually does not affect
management10,11
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:56 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000660
9/25

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Most nondisplaced or minimally displaced (Mason type I) radial head and neck fractures are
amenable to nonsurgical management.1,16
Type II fractures without block to rotation17
Contraindications
Type II fractures with mechanical block to motion (especially rotation)
Type III/type IV fractures
Associated elbow dislocation or fracture
Techniques/Procedures
Brief period of immobilization (7 to 10 days maximum) in a sling or posterior splint for pain
relief, followed by early ROM exercises.
Can consider aspiration of elbow hematoma with injection of local anesthetic to help with
acute pain.
Follow-up radiographs for nondisplaced fractures are not necessary if patient improves on
clinical examination.15
Outcomes
In general, excellent function with near-normal elbow ROM.
Type II fractures without mechanical block can have persistent symptoms, with up to a 12%
early failure rate.17
Surgical Management
Indications
Type III/type IV fractures
Type II fractures with mechanical block to motion
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:56 PM
AAOS | Radial Head and Neck Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000660
10/25

Substantial articular comminution
Associated elbow dislocation, terrible triad injury, distal humerus fracture
Open fracture

Indications
Surgical indications for radial head fractures are somewhat controversial. In general,
open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) is offered to patients with a radial head/neck
fracture that is displaced greater than or equal to 2 to 3 mm and that involve more than
30% of the radial head articular surface. Radial head/neck fractures with a true
mechanical block to forearm rotation should be managed surgically, regardless of size.
In patients with a concomitant elbow dislocation, the radial head/neck should be
surgically stabilized because it is an important secondary stabilizer of the elbow.
Contraindications
Medical comorbidities that prevent safe surgical management
Techniques/Procedures
Patient Positioning
In general, surgical procedures can be performed with the patient positioned supine, lateral,
or prone with a tourniquet.
Patient positioning depends on concomitant injuries and the need for other procedures.
Fluoroscopy can be placed at the head or the foot, depending on surgeon preference.
Surgical Approaches
Isolated radial head/neck fractures can be managed via a lateral or posterior approach.

Surgical Approaches
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:56 PM
AAOS | Radial Head and Neck Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000660
11/25

A lateral approach allows for easy evaluation of the radial head fracture and the lateral
ulnar collateral ligament (LUCL) complex. The two most common surgical intervals used
are the Kocher interval (split between the extensor carpi ulnaris and the anconeus;
Figure 7) and the Kaplan interval (split between the extensor carpi radialis brevis and the
extensor digitorum communis; Figure 8). The Kocher interval affords a more extensile
approach proximally because it can be extended as a lateral column approach to
manage any capitellar pathology. The Kocher interval generally decreases the risk of
injury to the posterior interosseous nerve; however, the approach is associated with a
risk of destabilization of the LUCL and is limited distally because of the posterior
interosseous nerve. The Kaplan interval affords direct access to the radial head/neck
without risk to the LUCL and can be extended distally to manage any pathology of the
radial shaft; however, the approach is associated with an increased risk of posterior
interosseous nerve injury. In patients with elbow instability, the LUCL usually is avulsed
off its humeral insertion, allowing access through a lateral window. A posterior incision
with large skin flaps can be used to address lateral- and medial-sided elbow pathology, if
necessary.
Figure 7 Illustration of the elbow shows the limited Kocher approach between the
anconeus and the extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU). ECRB = extensor carpi radialis brevis,
ECRL = extensor carpi radialis longus, EDC = extensor digitorum communis. (Reproduced
with permission from Patterson SD, Bain GI, Mehta JA: Surgical approaches to the elbow.
Clin Orthop Relat Res 2000;370:19-33.)

Figure 8 Illustration of the elbow shows the Kaplan approach between the extensor
digitorum communis (EDC) and the extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis (ECRB).
ECRL = extensor carpi radialis longus, ECU = extensor carpi ulnaris. (Reproduced with
permission from Patterson SD, Bain GI, Mehta JA: Surgical approaches to the elbow. Clin
Orthop Relat Res 2000;(370):19-33.
Surgical Procedures
ORIF8,18-20
Indications
Simple, partial articular fractures
Less than three displaced fragments
Screws (Figures 9 and 10)

Figure 9 Images of the elbow of a 31-year-old man. AP radiograph (A), lateral radiograph (B),
and three-dimensional CT reconstruction image (C) show a partial, articular radial head
fracture. The patient underwent open reduction and internal fixation of the displaced
fragment. A substantial chondral injury to the capitellum and an avulsion of the lateral
collateral ligament were observed intraoperatively and repaired. AP (D) and lateral (E)
radiographs obtained 3 months postoperatively demonstrate anatomic fixation. The patient
had occasional discomfort but had returned to work as a truck driver. Elbow range of motion

2013, pp 531-541.)

Figure 10 Images of the elbow of a 31-year-old man who worked as heavy manual laborer.
AP radiograph (A), lateral radiograph (B), and three-dimensional CT reconstruction image (C)
show a completely articular fracture of the radial head. The patient underwent open
reduction and internal fixation, with bouquet fixation of the radial head fragments to each
other and to the shaft. AP (D) and lateral (E) radiographs obtained 5 months postoperatively
demonstrate the fixation construct. Elbow range of motion was from 17° to 144°, with 70° of
pronation and 85° of supination. (Reproduced from Yoon A, King GJW: Radial head and neck
fractures, in Nicholson GP, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Shoulder and Elbow, ed 4.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2013, pp 531-541.)
Mini-fragment screws (2.4 or 2.0 mm) or headless screws with differential pitch (eg, Herbert
screw, headless compression screw) should be countersunk to prevent screw prominence.
Plates (radial neck)
Mini-fragment plates should be placed in the safe zone (Figure 2).
Radial head arthroplasty (RHA)14,18,21-27
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:56 PM
AAOS | Radial Head and Neck Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000660
15/25

Indications
Complete articular fractures
More than– three fracture fragments
Articular comminution
Radial head fracture fixation is associated with a higher failure rate in patients with elbow
instability.
Radial head excision6,7,28
Not commonly performed because of the role of radial head as an important stabilizer of the
elbow
Results in increased carrying angle at the elbow and proximal radial migration
Consider as salvage treatment option

Surgical Procedures
After the fracture fragments are identified, they should be reduced and secured using
Kirschner wires or compression screws. Screws are the preferred fixation method to
minimize impingement in the proximal radioulnar joint. Screw configuration can be
parallel to the joint in patients with a B-type fracture or aiming off-axis into the
medullary canal in patients with a C-type fracture. If a plate is necessary, it should be
contoured to match the patient’s anatomy and placed in the safe zone. Low-profile mini-
fragment plates should be used to minimize impingement. Surgeons should ensure that
hardware does not articulate with the proximal radioulnar joint or cause any mechanical
block.
Patient positioning and surgical approach for RHA are similar to that for ORIF. Optimal
sizing of the radial head prosthesis is necessary to avoid complications, such as pain and
postoperative stiffness14,21,24 (Figure 11). The articular fragments of the fracture should
be retained to help size the radial head prosthesis. The lesser of the two diameters of
the oval native radial head should be used to determine the diameter of the circular
arthroplasty. Implant length also should be determined by inspecting the resected radial
head. The prosthesis should articulate within the lesser sigmoid notch (2 mm distal to
the tip of the coronoid). Fluoroscopy should be used to confirm the length and size of
the radial head prosthesis. A lateral fluoroscopic image aids in assessing the diameter in
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:56 PM
AAOS | Radial Head and Neck Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000660
16/25

relation to the capitellum. An AP fluoroscopic image can be obtained to ensure that the
radial head is not replaced with a prosthesis that is too large (overstuffing the joint),
evaluating the symmetry and congruence of the ulnohumeral joint line specifically to
avoid pinching on the medial side. The elbow should be taken through ROM, with
stability testing performed. The radial head should track congruently against the
capitellum throughout ROM. The most common radial head replacement prosthesis
used is a modular, metallic, smooth-stem, noncemented prosthesis.14,26
Outcomes of ORIF and RHA generally are favorable and dependent on concomitant
injuries.
Figure 11 Images of the elbow of the dominant arm of a 60-year-old woman. AP
radiograph (A), lateral radiograph (B), and three-dimensional CT reconstruction image (C)
show a highly comminuted and displaced, completely articular radial head fracture. AP
(D) and lateral (E) radiographs obtained 3 months postoperatively demonstrate that the
patient underwent radial head arthroplasty with the use of a modular, smooth-stemmed
design. The implant length appears to be correct because the proximal aspect of the

17/25

metal implant articulates at the proximal aspect of the radial notch, the medial
ulnohumeral joint is parallel, and the lateral ulnohumeral joint space does not widen.
Typical mild radiolucency is observed around the implant stem. The patient returned to
normal activity and had full range of motion with no pain. (Reproduced from Yoon A,

Update: Shoulder and Elbow, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2013, pp 531-541.)
Postoperative Management
Initiate early active ROM within 7 to 14 days postoperatively29
Progression dependent on associated injuries and residual instability

Postoperative Management
Postoperative rehabilitation in patients with elbow trauma is a challenge, especially in
patients with terrible triad injuries. Isometric exercises and antigravity active extension
may be helpful in patients with residual subluxation (drop sign) in the early
postoperative period (Figure 12). This is easiest and safest if performed in the supine
position. In general, early combined supination and extension should be avoided in
patients with elbow instability and varus-producing moments. At six weeks
postoperatively, more aggressive ROM and strengthening exercises can be initiated
based on the patient’s injury pattern.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:56 PM
AAOS | Radial Head and Neck Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000660
18/25

Figure 12 Lateral elbow radiograph demonstrates the drop sign. (Courtesy of Alexander
Aleem, MD, St. Louis, MO.)
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Isolated fractures heal best with early mobilization after 7 to 10 days postoperatively.
Hardware should be applied to the safe zone.
Radial head fractures with three or more fragments are associated with a higher incidence of
unsatisfactory results after ORIF. Consider replacement rather than fixation for such fractures.
Radial head excision alone should not be performed in patients with other destabilizing
injuries, especially medial collateral ligament insufficiency.
Complications
Stiffness/Osteoarthritis
Stiffness (especially loss of supination) is common after surgical management.
More commonly associated with concomitant injuries
Radiocapitellar arthritis (Figure 13) is a common radiographic finding but is not correlated with
poor functional outcomes.17 Symptomatic capitellar wear is associated with overstuffing of the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:56 PM
AAOS | Radial Head and Neck Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000660
19/25

joint.
Figure 13 AP radiograph of an elbow in which press-fit radial head arthroplasty was performed
demonstrates osteolysis, chondral degeneration, and displacement. (Reproduced with
permission from Agyeman KD, Damodar D, Watkins I, Dodds SD: Does radial head implant
fixation affect functional outcomes? A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Shoulder Elbow
Surg 2019;28[1]:126-130.)

Stiffness/Osteoarthritis
Postoperative stiffness is the most common complication of surgical management and
may be caused by various factors, including prominent hardware, improper implant
sizing, capsular contracture, and heterotopic ossification. Soft-tissue stiffness usually can
be managed initially via physical therapy with the use of static or dynamic braces.
Surgical treatment may be necessary in patients with residual stiffness that does not
respond to physical therapy and bracing and patients who have stiffness with a firm
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:56 PM
AAOS | Radial Head and Neck Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000660
20/25

endpoint. In addition, heterotopic ossification causing a mechanical block may require
surgical management.
Nonunion/Malunion
Asymptomatic malunion/nonunion is common after nonsurgical and surgical
management.8,20,30
If associated with substantial pain or stiffness, radial head excision or arthroplasty can be
considered.
Pain
Pain usually is associated with elbow stiffness or overstuffing of joint during RHA14,18,24
Infection
Infection is rare after isolated ORIF or RHA.
More common with higher energy injuries, open fracture, or substantial associated soft-tissue
injuries.
Fracture
Fracture displacement (occurs in <5% of patients)
Hardware Failure
Failure of ORIF hardware is rare.8,19,26,27
Radiolucencies are common around stem of radial head prosthesis in patients with a
noncemented smooth stems but are not associated with pain.23
Hardware Malpositioning
Overstuffing the joint may lead to pain and stiffness. The placement of plates and screws
within the safe zone leads to decreased forearm rotation.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:56 PM
AAOS | Radial Head and Neck Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000660
21/25

Instability
Uncommon if associated elbow injuries are managed and the radial head is not excised.
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Posterior interosseous nerve injury most common after surgical management
Higher incidence of neurovascular injury in patients with higher energy injuries and associated
elbow dislocations
Other Complications
Proximal migration of radius after radial head excision may lead to pain in the elbow and wrist
(ulnar impaction).
Mark as Complete
